lead: A fluid particle can speed up for two reasons: the velocity at its fixed point changes with time, or the particle drifts to a place where the velocity is different. The first is the local part. The second is the convective part. Their sum is the material derivative, the true acceleration of the particle. Engineers use it to size pumps and pipes, to read pitot tubes in moving air, and to check whether a bend in a pipeline will load its supports. The same derivative appears in weather models and in CFD software.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.1 for the Eulerian field view, Chapter 2.2 for steady and uniform flow, and Chapter 2.3 for streamlines.

blocks.text: Take a velocity field V = u i + v j + w k. u, v, w are the velocity components in the x, y, z directions, in m/s. x, y, z are fixed coordinates in metres. t is time in seconds. A fluid particle is not fixed. In dt seconds it moves dx = u dt, dy = v dt, dz = w dt. Its velocity changes for two reasons: time passes at the point, and the particle moves to a new point.

blocks.where: a is acceleration in m/s²; V = u i + v j + w k is velocity in m/s; x, y, z are metres; t is seconds. ∂V/∂t is the local part. The three u, v, w terms form the convective part.

blocks.text: The local part ∂V/∂t is the change at a fixed point. The convective part is the change caused by the particle moving to a place where the field is different. Some syllabi call DV/Dt the substantial derivative or Stokes derivative. In Cartesian components:
ax = ∂u/∂t + u ∂u/∂x + v ∂u/∂y + w ∂u/∂z; ay = ∂v/∂t + u ∂v/∂x + v ∂v/∂y + w ∂v/∂z; az = ∂w/∂t + u ∂w/∂x + v ∂w/∂y + w ∂w/∂z
blocks.where: ax, ay, az are acceleration components in m/s²; u, v, w are velocity components in m/s; x, y, z are metres; t is seconds.

blocks.text: In steady flow ∂V/∂t = 0 at every point, so the local part vanishes. The convective part can still be large. Water speeding up as a pipe narrows is a steady flow with particle acceleration. In uniform flow the velocity is the same at every point at a given instant, so all ∂/∂x, ∂/∂y, ∂/∂z terms vanish and the convective part is zero. The local part can remain if the whole field changes with time.

Along a streamline, split acceleration into tangent and normal directions. For steady flow, the tangent part is V dV/ds. The normal part is V²/R, directed toward the centre of curvature. This normal term is centripetal acceleration. A fluid element on a curved path has it even at constant speed. R is the radius of curvature in metres.

blocks.where: a_s is acceleration along the streamline in m/s²; a_n is normal acceleration toward the centre of curvature in m/s²; V is speed in m/s; s is distance along the streamline in m; R is radius of curvature in m.

sections.h3: How to compute acceleration at a point

blocks.text: Work only with the field. Do not follow a guessed particle path. The coordinates x, y, z and time t are independent variables. The chain rule supplies the convective terms because the particle's x, y, z change with t. A common mistake is to differentiate u with respect to t while holding x, y, z fixed and stop there. That gives only the local part.

items: Write u, v, w from the field. Set any missing component to zero.
Put the given x, y, z, t into u, v, w to get the velocity there in m/s.
Find ∂u/∂t, ∂u/∂x, ∂u/∂y, ∂u/∂z and the same derivatives of v and w at that point.
Substitute into the three Cartesian component formulas.
Write the acceleration vector with units m/s².

figure.caption: The velocity field feeds two parallel parts. The local part uses time at a fixed point; the convective part uses spatial slopes, and both add to the material derivative.

spec.title: Total acceleration
spec.aria: A block diagram shows velocity field branching into local and convective parts, which combine into total acceleration as the material derivative.

examples.question: A flow field has u = 3x + 2t and v = 4y, with u and v in m/s, x and y in metres, and t in seconds. The z component w is zero. Find ax and ay at x = 1 m, y = 2 m, t = 1 s.
examples.answer: At the given point, a = (17 i + 32 j) m/s², so ax = 17 m/s² and ay = 32 m/s².
examples.check:
x = 1.0
y = 2.0
t = 1.0
u = 3*x + 2*t
v = 4*y
ax = 2 + u*3
ay = v*4
print(ax)
print(ay)

traps: Steady flow does not mean zero acceleration. ∂V/∂t is zero, but u ∂u/∂x and similar convective terms can be large.
Do not differentiate u = 3x + 2t along a guessed path. x, y, z, t are independent field coordinates; the chain rule adds u ∂u/∂x and the other convective terms.
Keep units: ∂u/∂t is in m/s², ∂u/∂x is in s⁻¹, and u ∂u/∂x is in m/s². Do not treat ∂u/∂x as an acceleration.
Uniform flow kills only the convective part. Unsteady uniform flow still has local acceleration. Steady flow kills only the local part.
Curved streamlines give normal acceleration V²/R even when speed is constant. Straight streamlines have infinite R and zero normal term.

quiz.q: Define the local and convective parts of acceleration.
quiz.a: Local part = ∂V/∂t at a fixed point. Convective part = (V·∇)V, caused by the particle moving to a point where the velocity is different.

quiz.q: Why must acceleration use the material derivative, not just ∂V/∂t?
quiz.a: A particle moves through the field, so its velocity changes both with time at a point and with position. ∂V/∂t misses the change caused by moving to a new point.

quiz.q: For u = 2x + t and v = 3y, find ax and ay at x = 2 m, y = 1 m, t = 3 s. Take w = 0.
Can a particle accelerate in steady flow? Give an example.
quiz.a: Yes. The local part is zero, but the convective part can be nonzero. Water accelerating into a narrower pipe is one example; flow round a bend also has centripetal acceleration V²/R.

quiz.q: Steady flow along a curved streamline has V = 10 m/s and R = 5 m. Find the normal acceleration.
quiz.a: a_n = V²/R = (10)²/5 = 20 m/s², directed toward the centre of curvature.

quiz.q: Which part of DV/Dt vanishes in uniform flow?
quiz.a: The convective part vanishes, because all spatial derivatives of velocity are zero.

quiz.q: What is the particle acceleration in an unsteady uniform flow?
quiz.a: Only the local part remains. The convective part is zero because the velocity is the same at every point at a given instant, so a = ∂V/∂t.

beyond: Not for the exam. CFD solvers store the velocity field and compute local plus convective terms on a mesh; the same split appears in the Navier–Stokes equations. Weather forecasts advect momentum and heat with the convective operator. Blood flow in curved arteries uses the V²/R term to estimate wall stress.
